chapter: Minton's, Louis Armstrong and the South
title: Sid Catlett coaches him through Armstrong's book
summary: Big Sid, leaving for Goodman, drilled Clarke through Armstrong's repertoire at the Renaissance, so he played it flawlessly at his first job in Memphis.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: And you mean to say Louis hired you,
heard you and hired you? He said, "That man is modern."
Yeah, but where did he hear you?
Now, here's what happened. Big Sidney went with Benny Goodman. He joined Benny Goodman in Detroit.
Yeah.
Remember?
Yeah.

Well, Big Sidney was with the band. So he said, "Kenny, Pops digs you." Now, Pops had heard me play around with Louis Russell and all these bands, at the Apollo, because he was sweet on this little girl he married. She was a chorus girl at the Apollo Theater, so Louis used to be around a lot.
Yeah.
And so Big Sid took me to the Renaissance and set up his drums. He set up his drums with the whole repertoire, Louis' whole repertoire, and we went through the whole repertoire, for about --
You seem to have had the most beautiful experiences.
It's unbelievable.
It is. It's extraordinary.
I just fall on my knees and pray all the time. You know? Which I've been doing since I was 12. But

Louis -- I mean Sid, he had been listening to me at Minton's, you know. He was the first one that put the word out. He said, "Man, that little cat is playing something out there. You cats better watch it, man. That little cat out there is mean." You know. So he took me to the Renaissance Casino and set up his drums and brought the whole repertoire, Louis' whole repertoire, and we went through that book at least five or six times every day, for about four or five days. And he says, "Okay, I look, I'm going to join Benny," and he went to Detroit. And I joined Louis and we went to -- let's see, our first job was in Gary, Indiana. No, no, that wasn't the first one. The first one was in Memphis, at the W. C. Handy Theater, or Hall, whatever you call it. So Louis looked at me and said, "All right, Gizzard?" I said, "Yeah, everything's all right, Pops." He said, "Okay." So he started playing, "Skeleton in the Closet," and, "Strutting with some Barbecue", and I knew it like I had been playing it for years, and he couldn't believe it. He said, "Gizzard, where did you learn those?" I said, "I've just been listening." But I wouldn't tell him.
(Laughter)
I wouldn't tell him that Big Sid had took me over, because he would figure that there was a little conspiracy, you know.
Yeah, sure. How funny.
I said, "I've just been listening."
So he said, 'Doggone it, you play it like you've been playing it for years.' I said, 'Oh, thanks, Pops.' So we left there.
The guys must have been surprised, because when they hired you the guys must have been a little worried.
Well Joe, Joe Garland, you know, I worked with him with Edgar Hayes' band.
Yeah.
So he kind of backed it up and said, 'Yeah, Pops, that's the man,' you know, because he knew my work.
Yeah.

And well, we left Memphis and we played Gary, Indiana. That's the one that really cinched it, because he reached back in the book for things he thought I'd never heard before. But Sid took me through everything.
That's a really unbelievable story, isn't it?
